newsitem.title: COTE D'IVOIRE: Donors arrive for crucial Ivory Coast aid talks.
newsitem.headline: Donors arrive for crucial Ivory Coast aid talks.

text.p: Teams from the World Bank and International Monetary Fund (IMF) were scheduled to arrive in Ivory Coast this weekend for meetings with the government on a new structural adjustment plan.

Donor sources predicted tough talks, dealing, amongst other things, with fiscal and commodity sector reforms, poverty reduction plans and infrastructure improvements, as part of a renewed Enhanced Structural Adjustment Facility (ESAF).

Jean-Louis Sarbib, one of the World Bank's vice-presidents for Africa, preferred to put the emphasis on what Ivory Coast had achieved since the 50 percent devaluation of its CFA franc in 1994 ended a recession lasting since the mid-1980s.

"Ivory Coast has gone through one of the worst recessions that any country has known. Some people have compared it to the great recessions (in the West) of the 1920s," Sarbib told Reuters in an interview.
"What they have done, and done very well since 1994, is put the country on a growth path again," he said.
The government has put growth at 7.1 percent in 1995 and 6.8 percent in 1996, and is predicting seven percent this year.
Critics have argued that this spurt in growth has benefited only a few, and that the gap between the richest and poorest has widened considerably since the early 1990s.

One media report, purportedly based on a World Bank study, said the percentage of the Ivorian population with an income below the relative povery threshold of 144,800 CFA francs ($230) per year rose to 36.8 percent in 1995 from 10 percent in 1985.
The government has protested at the report, and the World Bank is investigating to see whether the partial results from a study were misused.
"The concern that everyone has, including the government, is to see that this growth is equitably shared," Sarbib said.
The World Bank wanted to see programmes that created jobs in urban areas, and reduced poverty in rural areas, Sarbib said.
Ivory Coast is the world's biggest producer of cocoa, and Africa's biggest robusta coffee producer.

Donors are increasing pressure on the government to liberalise the marketing of its cocoa and coffee crops, with producer prices set by the market, rather than by the state commodities board, the Caisse de Stabilisation (Caistab).
The government has agreed sweeping reforms along these lines in the coffee sector, but donors see slower progress on cocoa.
Sarbib declined to go into details on the cocoa question, but said: "I think we're making progress."

Other donor sources were less optimistic. One pointed out there was a long agenda for the talks, due to last from around August 9 to 14, and it would be ambitious to expect agreement on all points in time for an IMF board meeting in early September.

Talks could continue in Hong Kong during the annual World Bank/IMF meetings from September 23-25, but this would delay a Paris Club agreement on debt reduction and affect Ivory Coast's chances of getting a comprehensive debt deal under the donor community's Heavily Indebted Poor Countries initiative.
Ivory Coast's previous three-year ESAF was agreed with the IMF in 1994, in the aftermath of the CFA franc devaluation. ($ = 630 CFA francs)
